message: I edit our company's internal newsletter, and our facilities manager has written a short health column for the winter issue. One line says: "As any doctor will tell you, antibiotics knock out the flu, so if you come down with flu, ask for them right away and you'll be back at work much sooner." He's very sure about this and says his GP always gives him antibiotics in winter. It seems sensible to me and it's a helpful tip for staff. Can we run the line as written?
response:
**No, please don't run that line.** It's medically wrong, and the advice could harm staff.

## What's wrong with it

- **Flu is caused by a virus, and antibiotics only work on bacteria.** They have no effect on the flu virus and won't make anyone better faster. This is standard medical advice, so "as any doctor will tell you" actually points the wrong way.
- **Unnecessary antibiotics carry real costs.**
  - **Side effects:** they can cause stomach upsets, thrush and allergic reactions.
  - **Antibiotic resistance:** every unnecessary course adds to it, which makes the drugs less effective when people genuinely need them.
- **Doctors may decline the request.** Telling staff to "ask for them right away" sets them up to push for a prescription their doctor will rightly refuse.

## Why his GP may have prescribed them

Your facilities manager probably isn't making this up. A GP may give antibiotics when flu or a cold leads to a **secondary bacterial infection**, such as a chest infection, pneumonia or sinusitis. In that case the antibiotics treat the complication, not the flu. Over several winters, it's easy to remember that as "antibiotics for flu."

## What actually helps with flu

- **The flu vaccine** is by far the best way to avoid losing work days to flu. This is a genuinely useful tip for a company newsletter, especially if staff can get it through work.
- **Antiviral medicines** exist for flu and can shorten it slightly. They're usually prescribed only for people at higher risk of complications, and they work best when started within about 48 hours of symptoms.
- **Rest, fluids and paracetamol or ibuprofen** for fever and aches are the treatment for most healthy adults.
- **Staying home while unwell** helps you recover and stops flu spreading through the office.

## Suggested replacement line

> *Flu is caused by a virus, so antibiotics won't help. Your best protection is the flu jab. If you do catch flu, rest, drink plenty of fluids and stay home so it doesn't spread. Contact your GP or pharmacist if you're in a higher-risk group, if your symptoms are severe, or if you start to feel worse after improving, as this can be a sign of a chest infection.*

The final point gives staff the helpful part of his experience: when it's genuinely worth seeing a doctor.

To keep things smooth with the author, you could tell him the column is being checked against standard health guidance, such as your national health service's flu page. Linking to that page at the end of the column would also be useful for readers.
